title: Jeremiah 5:1–9
context: Jeremiah 5:1–9 opens with the LORD telling his hearers to run through the streets of Jerusalem and look for one person who does justly and seeks truth, so that he might pardon the city. The search fails. In verses 3–5 Jeremiah speaks to the LORD and then reports his own search: he first assumes the poor simply do not know God’s way, then goes to the great men, only to find that they too have broken the yoke. The LORD answers with images of wild animals attacking the cities and asks how he can pardon a people who swear by false gods and commit adultery. The language of verses 7–8 describes both literal sexual sin and spiritual unfaithfulness, and it should be read soberly. The unit closes with the LORD’s question whether he should not punish such a nation. Both traditions read the chapter as a call to repentance set before judgment, during the final decades before Babylon’s conquest of Jerusalem (compare 2 Kings 24–25 and Jeremiah 39 and 52).

verses.text: “Run back and forth through the streets of Jerusalem, and see now, and know, and seek in its wide places, if you can find a man, if there is anyone who does justly, who seeks truth, then I will pardon her.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD tells his hearers to search Jerusalem for one person who does justly and seeks truth, and he will pardon the city. Arminian readers see God’s genuine willingness to forgive, so that judgment comes only after he has sought every reason to show mercy.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree that the verse displays God’s patience and readiness to pardon. Both traditions note the echo of Abraham’s plea for Sodom (Genesis 18:23–32) and read the failed search as showing how deep the city’s corruption has become.

verses.text: Though they say, ‘As the LORD lives,’ surely they swear falsely.”
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says that though the people swear by his name, they swear falsely. Arminians see religious language without truth, where outward use of God’s name hides a heart that does not honor him.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the verse as exposing empty religion. Both traditions treat this as shared ground: using the LORD’s name in oaths does not make a person faithful if their words and lives are false.

verses.text: O LORD, don’t your eyes look on truth? You have stricken them, but they were not grieved. You have consumed them, but they have refused to receive correction. They have made their faces harder than a rock. They have refused to return.
verses.arminianNotes: Jeremiah speaks to the LORD, saying God looks for truth, but though he struck the people, they refused correction and hardened their faces. Arminian readers see real human refusal of God’s discipline, which made their judgment just.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree that the people are responsible for refusing correction, and they see hardening as both a human act and part of God’s righteous dealings. Both traditions affirm that God’s discipline was meant to bring them back, and that they would not return.

verses.text: Then I said, “Surely these are poor. They are foolish; for they don’t know the LORD’s way, nor the law of their God.
verses.arminianNotes: Jeremiah says that surely these are only the poor, who are foolish and do not know the LORD’s way. Arminians see Jeremiah first trying to excuse the people, assuming their ignorance comes from lack of teaching.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the prophet’s compassion in his first assumption. Both traditions note that Jeremiah’s search moves on to the leaders, showing that the problem is not only ignorance but rebellion throughout society.

verses.text: I will go to the great men and will speak to them, for they know the way of the LORD, and the law of their God.” But these with one accord have broken the yoke, and burst the bonds.
verses.arminianNotes: Jeremiah says he will go to the great men, who know the LORD’s way, but they have all broken the yoke and burst the bonds. Arminian readers see deliberate rebellion by those who knew better, which makes their guilt greater.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the image of the broken yoke as the rejection of God’s rule. Both traditions hold that knowledge brings greater responsibility (compare Luke 12:48), and that the leaders’ rebellion is especially serious.

verses.text: Therefore a lion out of the forest will kill them. A wolf of the evenings will destroy them. A leopard will watch against their cities. Everyone who goes out there will be torn in pieces, because their transgressions are many and their backsliding has increased.
verses.arminianNotes: A lion, a wolf, and a leopard will attack the cities, because the people’s sins and backsliding are many. Arminians see vivid images of coming judgment, which follows from the people’s persistent unfaithfulness.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and read the animals as figures for invading enemies or for disaster in general. Both traditions note that the verse ties the judgment directly to the people’s transgressions, so that it is just and not arbitrary.

verses.text: “How can I pardon you? Your children have forsaken me, and sworn by what are no gods. When I had fed them to the full, they committed adultery, and assembled themselves in troops at the prostitutes’ houses.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD asks how he can pardon a people who forsook him, swore by false gods, and after being fed went after prostitutes. Arminian readers see both literal sexual sin and spiritual unfaithfulness, and they note that God’s question is a lament, not indifference.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the image of adultery as a common prophetic picture of idolatry alongside real moral sin. Both traditions note the painful contrast that God had fed them to the full, and they read his question as showing that pardon without repentance is impossible.

verses.text: They were as fed horses roaming at large. Everyone neighed after his neighbor’s wife.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD compares the people to well-fed horses, each one lusting after his neighbor’s wife. Arminians see a blunt picture of unrestrained desire, which Scripture names plainly so that sin is seen for what it is.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and read the verse as describing real breaking of the seventh commandment (Exodus 20:14) within a wider culture of unfaithfulness. Both traditions treat the image soberly, as a call to repentance rather than to curiosity.

verses.text: Shouldn’t I punish them for these things?” says the LORD. “Shouldn’t my soul be avenged on such a nation as this?
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD asks whether he should not punish them and be avenged on such a nation. Arminian readers see God’s justice, which must answer persistent rebellion, while noting that the question form invites the hearers to agree that judgment is right.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see God’s justice as an expression of his holiness. Both traditions note that the same question returns in 5:29 and 9:9, and they read it as showing that God’s judgment is reasoned and righteous.
